questions.question: Among the following substituted cyclohexyl carbocations, which one is stabilized by the maximum number of hyperconjugative structures?

For the 1-tert-butylcyclohexyl cation, the tert-butyl group provides 0 $\alpha$-hydrogens. Total $\alpha$-hydrogens = $0 + 4 = 4$.

Therefore, the 1-methylcyclohexyl cation has the maximum number of $\alpha$-hydrogens and is stabilized by the maximum number of hyperconjugative structures.

questions.question: 2-Butene is thermodynamically more stable than 1-butene. Which of the following primary electronic displacement effects is responsible for this difference in stability?
questions.solution:
The stability of alkenes is primarily determined by the number of $\alpha$-hydrogens attached to the $sp^2$ hybridized carbon atoms, which participate in hyperconjugation.

2-Butene ($\text{CH}_3-\text{CH}=\text{CH}-\text{CH}_3$) has 6 $\alpha$-hydrogens, leading to more extensive hyperconjugation.

1-Butene ($\text{CH}_2=\text{CH}-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_3$) has only 2 $\alpha$-hydrogens.

The greater the number of hyperconjugative structures, the more stable the alkene. While the $+I$ effect is present, hyperconjugation is the dominating factor for alkene stability. The electromeric effect is a temporary effect requiring an attacking reagent, and the resonance effect requires an extended conjugated $\pi$ system which is absent in these simple alkenes.

questions.question: The correct decreasing order of the basic strength of ethyl substituted amines and ammonia in aqueous solution is:
questions.solution:
In aqueous solution, the basic strength of amines depends on the combined effect of the inductive effect (+I), solvation (hydrogen bonding with water), and steric hindrance.

For ethyl substituted amines, the larger size of the ethyl group compared to the methyl group causes steric hindrance to play a more significant role, altering the balance between solvation and the +I effect.

The resulting order of basicity for ethylamines in aqueous solution is secondary > tertiary > primary > ammonia. Therefore, the correct decreasing order is $(\text{C}_2\text{H}_5)_2\text{NH} > (\text{C}_2\text{H}_5)_3\text{N} > \text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{NH}_2 > \text{NH}_3$.

Answer: $(\text{C}_2\text{H}_5)_2\text{NH} > (\text{C}_2\text{H}_5)_3\text{N} > \text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{NH}_2 > \text{NH}_3$

questions.question: Among the following nitrogenous compounds, which one is the most difficult to protonate?
questions.solution:
The ease of protonation of a compound depends on the availability of the lone pair of electrons on the basic atom (nitrogen, in this case).

In methylamine and dimethylamine, the alkyl (methyl) groups exert an electron-donating inductive effect (+I effect), which increases the electron density on the nitrogen atom. This makes their lone pairs more available for protonation compared to ammonia.

In aniline, the nitrogen atom is directly attached to a benzene ring. The lone pair of electrons on the nitrogen atom is delocalized into the aromatic ring through resonance. This delocalization significantly decreases the electron density on the nitrogen atom, making the lone pair least available for protonation.

Therefore, aniline is the most difficult to protonate among the given options.

Answer: Aniline

questions.question: What is the minimum number of carbon atoms required for an aliphatic, non-cyclic ketone to exhibit metamerism?
questions.solution:
Metamerism arises due to different alkyl chains on either side of a polyvalent functional group. For ketones, the functional group is the carbonyl group ($-\text{CO}-$), which is divalent.

Let us check the homologous series of aliphatic ketones:
With 3 carbon atoms: $\text{CH}_3-\text{CO}-\text{CH}_3$ (Propanone). No other arrangement of alkyl groups around the carbonyl carbon is possible.
With 4 carbon atoms: $\text{CH}_3-\text{CO}-\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$ (Butan-2-one). No other arrangement is possible.
With 5 carbon atoms: The alkyl groups can be a methyl and a propyl group, giving $\text{CH}_3-\text{CO}-\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$ (Pentan-2-one), or two ethyl groups, giving $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2-\text{CO}-\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$ (Pentan-3-one). These two compounds are metamers.

Thus, a minimum of 5 carbon atoms is required for an aliphatic ketone to exhibit metamerism.

Answer: 5

questions.solution:
The stability of alkyl carbocations is determined by the number of $\alpha$-hydrogens (hyperconjugation) and inductive effects.

III. 2-Methylpropan-2-yl cation (tert-butyl cation) has 3 methyl groups attached to the positively charged carbon, giving $3 + 3 + 3 = 9$ $\alpha$-hydrogens.

II. 4-Chloro-2-methylbutan-2-yl cation also has $3 + 3 + 2 = 8$ $\alpha$-hydrogens. However, the presence of the electronegative chlorine atom exerts a $-I$ (electron-withdrawing inductive) effect, which decreases the electron density on the positively charged carbon, making it less stable than I.

Therefore, the correct decreasing order of stability is III > I > II.

questions.question:
Consider the following compounds:
I. Cyclohexanol
II. Phenol
III. $p$-Nitrophenol
IV. $p$-Methoxyphenol

The correct decreasing order of their ease of protonation is:
questions.solution:
The ease of protonation (basicity) depends on the availability of the lone pair of electrons on the oxygen atom.

In cyclohexanol (I), the oxygen atom is attached to an $sp^3$ hybridized carbon, and its lone pairs are fully localized. This makes it the most electron-rich and easiest to protonate among the given compounds.

In phenol (II), $p$-nitrophenol (III), and $p$-methoxyphenol (IV), the oxygen atom is attached to an aromatic ring, and its lone pair is delocalized into the ring via resonance, making them less basic than cyclohexanol.

Among the aromatic compounds, substituents affect the electron density on oxygen. The methoxy group in $p$-methoxyphenol (IV) exerts an electron-donating resonance effect (+R), which increases the electron density on the oxygen atom compared to phenol (II).

Conversely, the nitro group in $p$-nitrophenol (III) exerts strong electron-withdrawing resonance and inductive effects (-R, -I), significantly decreasing the electron density on the oxygen atom and making it the most difficult to protonate.

Therefore, the correct decreasing order of ease of protonation is I > IV > II > III. Note that the reverse order (III > II > IV > I) represents their acidic strength.

Answer: I > IV > II > III

The stability of carbocations is determined by the electron-donating effects (resonance, hyperconjugation, and inductive effects) of the attached groups.

Normally, when an organic compound containing both nitrogen and sulphur is fused with sodium, sodium thiocyanate ($\text{NaSCN}$) is formed, which provides the thiocyanate ion ($\text{SCN}^{-}$).

However, when an excess of sodium metal is used during the fusion process, the sodium thiocyanate decomposes to form sodium cyanide and sodium sulphide.

As a result, the extract will predominantly contain cyanide ($\text{CN}^{-}$) and sulphide ($\text{S}^{2-}$) ions instead of thiocyanate ions.

Consider the following nitrogenous bases:
Aniline, Ammonia, Methylamine, and Dimethylamine.

Which of the following represents the correct decreasing order of their $\text{p}K_b$ values in aqueous solution?
questions.solution:
The basic strength of amines depends on the availability of the lone pair on the nitrogen atom for protonation.

In aqueous solution, aliphatic amines are stronger bases than ammonia due to the $+\text{I}$ effect of alkyl groups. Among methylamines, dimethylamine is a stronger base than methylamine due to a combination of $+\text{I}$ effect, solvation, and steric factors.

Aniline is a weaker base than ammonia because the lone pair on nitrogen is delocalised into the benzene ring through resonance.

Thus, the decreasing order of basic strength ($K_b$) is:
$\left(\text{CH}_3\right)_2\text{NH} > \text{CH}_3\text{NH}_2 > \text{NH}_3 > \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NH}_2$

Since $\text{p}K_b = -\log K_b$, a stronger base has a lower $\text{p}K_b$ value. Therefore, the decreasing order of $\text{p}K_b$ values is the exact reverse of the basic strength order:
$\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NH}_2 > \text{NH}_3 > \text{CH}_3\text{NH}_2 > \left(\text{CH}_3\right)_2\text{NH}$

Answer: $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NH}_2 > \text{NH}_3 > \text{CH}_3\text{NH}_2 > \left(\text{CH}_3\right)_2\text{NH}$
